name: One-nation conservatism
summary: One-nation conservatism is the British Tory tradition associated with Benjamin Disraeli, which defends the Crown, the House of Lords and the established Church while holding that the governing class owes the people social reform, so that the 'two nations' of rich and poor become one. In Disraeli's own speeches the Tory party is a national party drawn from all classes, whose objects are to maintain the institutions, uphold the empire and raise the condition of the people, including by sanitary and factory legislation. It is a patriotic, monarchical and Anglican doctrine that prefers class partnership to class conflict.
scope: Disraeli's one-nation Toryism as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy presents it (the 'two nations' of Sybil, the Reform Act of 1867 and the social legislation of his government), read through Disraeli's own texts: Sybil (1845), the preface to Coningsby (1844), his Church speeches of 1861-64 and his Manchester and Crystal Palace speeches of 1872. Later users of the label (Baldwin, Macmillan, Butler, Cameron) and the post-war consensus are described in Wikipedia and in works it cites (Dorey, Vincent, Heywood, Bochel), which could not be opened here (a bot check blocked the one open copy), so they are not covered. The SEP's general sections on conservatism belong to conservatism as a whole and are not used.

notes: Brought up to rules 5 as a later pass by the same model as the first pass (no other model was available to the run). The earlier answers rested mainly on Wikipedia and on general conservatism, so they were nulled unless Disraeli's own texts settle them. Disraeli's texts read: Sybil, the Coningsby preface, the Manchester and Crystal Palace speeches (1872), the Edinburgh Reform speech (1867, read in part) and the Church speeches (1861-64). Themes searched with no stated position found: economy (tax, welfare, markets, trade, ownership), liberty and crime, immigration and race, foreign affairs beyond empire, ecology, technology, gender and family. The 1870s social legislation is a record of one Conservative government among parties, not of the ideology as official doctrine, so it was not used as a record. Blocked or unopened: Bochel's 'One Nation Conservatism and social policy, 1951-64' (core.ac.uk bot check) and Williams on the Industrial Charter (OpenEdition bot check); the Industrial Charter text itself was not found open. The imperial-pride missing statement from the first pass stays declined; Disraeli's two statements on empire (Manchester, Crystal Palace) could be reconsidered by the statement pass.
